newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin aide under fire as Yeltsin surgery nears.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin aide under fire as Yeltsin surgery nears.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's chief of staff faced new accusations on Thursday that he is trying to usurp power, days before doctors meet to discuss when the Kremlin leader should have heart surgery.

U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who is expected to advise the Russian doctors who will operate on Yeltsin, said on Wednesday he would discuss the date of the operation in Moscow on Monday and that it could go ahead as early as next week.
But a political row around top Kremlin aide Anatoly Chubais has been deepening as the 65-year-old president undergoes tests this week in a sanatorium outside Moscow.

The communist head of the lower house of parliament on Wednesday called for Chubais, the chief of the Kremlin staff, to be sacked over the appointment of businessman Boris Berezovsky as deputy secretary of Yeltsin's advisory Security Council.

Many Russian newspapers backed State Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov's suggestion that Chubais had engineered the nomination of Berezovsky. Berezovsky's business interests range from car dealerships to television, but critics say he has no experience of security matters.
"A covert political coup has taken place in Russia since the presidential election (last July)," Pavel Varashchanov, Yeltsin's former press secretary, wrote in Komsomolskaya Pravda.

"All power is now concentrated in the hands of representatives of the clan headed by Anatoly Chubais. He already has the essential things to make the president and the prime minister reckon with his interests."
Yeltsin's four-month absence from the Kremlin has prompted talk of a fierce power struggle.

Chubais, brought into the Kremlin last July, is widely disliked, particularly by the opposition communists who attack the free-market economic reforms he helped to launch as a government minister before joining the Kremlin team.
Angered by Berezovsky's appointment, Seleznyov said he would not take part in a newly-established consultative council on which Chubais is also due to sit.

Yeltsin had hoped the four-member council, which also includes Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Yegor Stroyev, head of the upper chamber of parliament, would help avert the in-fighting that has plagued recent Russian politics.

Chernomyrdin said late on Wednesday that the council's first meeting would not go ahead as planned on Friday and would be put off until next week. He said the decision was made because Stroyev would not have been able to attend on Friday.
The presidential press service gave no new details of Yeltsin's health on Thursday. "The planned preparations for the operation are continuing," a spokesman said.
Doctors plan to bypass blocked cardiac arteries and improve the blood supply to his heart.

"We're shooting for next week, but I can't be any more specific than that because we'll probably be meeting on Monday with the medical team and making that decision," DeBakey told the British Broadcasting Corporation.

DeBakey said doctors were expecting three or four bypasses. He said Yeltsin should be able to resume normal duties within six weeks to two months if the operation succeeds. "He should be able to have another 10 years of good work life."
